meta.title: Cutting the cost of the last mile
meta.subtitle: Where regional delivery spend leaks, and what to change first
meta.author: Illustrative Advisory Group

blocks.note: All company names, figures and sources in this sample are invented to demonstrate the layouts.

blocks.title: Executive summary
blocks.lead: Northgate can lower cost per delivered parcel by roughly 11% within 12 months, without cutting service levels, by fixing three things in order: route density, depot dwell time and carrier mix.

figures.label: Projected reduction in cost per parcel (central case)
Annual saving in illustrative currency units

points: **Density, not distance, drives cost.** Routes below 62 stops per round account for 38% of mileage but only 21% of volume.[^1]
**Dwell time is the hidden queue.** Median parcels wait 5.3 hours between arrival and van loading at the three largest depots.[^2]
**Carrier mix is out of balance.** Third-party carriers cover 24% of volume at a unit cost 17% above in-house rounds on comparable routes.[^3]
**Sequencing matters.** Dwell-time fixes unlock capacity that makes the density redesign cheaper to deliver.

after.callout: Decisions requested: approve the Phase 1 pilot at two depots, release the routing-software budget, and agree the carrier renegotiation mandate.

blocks.title: Where the network stands
blocks.label: Section 01 — Baseline
blocks.intro: A picture of volumes, routes and unit costs across 14 depots, drawn from twelve months of operating data.

blocks.title: A network built for yesterday's volumes
blocks.lead: Northgate grew by acquisition. Its 14 depots, 212 daily rounds and five carrier contracts reflect the history of the business more than the shape of present demand.
items: Between 2023 and 2025 parcel volume grew 31%, while the number of rounds grew only 9%. The difference was absorbed by longer working days and by third-party carriers, which now handle roughly one parcel in four.[^1] Neither response is cheap. Overtime rose to 7.4% of paid hours, and the third-party rate card was last renegotiated in 2022.

items.note: A *round* is one driver's scheduled delivery run from a single depot. Figures here count rounds per weekday.
items.label: Definition

items: The network is not uniformly stretched. Four urban depots run dense, profitable rounds with more than 80 stops each. Eight regional depots run sparse rounds, and two coastal depots are seasonal. Averages hide this spread, which is why earlier cost reviews, which focused on network-wide benchmarks, found nothing to act on.

items.quote: The average round looks fine. Almost no round is average.

items: Route-level data covers 1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026 and was supplied by Northgate's operations team. Cost data was matched to routes using the finance cost-centre map.[^2] Where a depot could not supply scan timestamps, dwell time was estimated from gate logs, and those estimates are flagged in the appendix.

items.note: Three depots reported dwell time from gate logs, not parcel scans. See Appendix A.
items.label: Data quality

items: Long paragraphs, lists and subheads are expected in this layout: the text column keeps a comfortable measure, and margin notes remain beside the passage they qualify, even when a section runs onto a second page.

blocks.takeaway: Moving the 98 regional rounds from 58 to 62 stops would remove the cost penalty on most of them, without adding vehicles.

blocks.title: What is driving the cost
blocks.label: Section 02 — Diagnosis
blocks.intro: Three mechanisms explain most of the gap between Northgate's best and worst rounds.

blocks.title: Three mechanisms behind the gap
blocks.lead: Dwell time, route design and carrier mix interact. Treating them separately would understate the opportunity.
items: At the three largest depots the median parcel waits 5.3 hours between arrival and van loading. Part of that wait is deliberate sorting. Most is queueing behind late inbound trailers and a single manifest cut-off at 06:30.[^2] Late loading forces drivers to leave after 08:00, which pushes the last third of their stops into peak traffic.

Rounds are drawn on postcode boundaries set in 2019. Since then, two new housing developments and a logistics park have shifted demand. Three adjacent rounds in the north-east serve overlapping streets at different times of day, each with a low drop density.

bullets: Round boundaries unchanged since 2019 in 11 of 14 depots.
Median stop spacing 31% higher on regional rounds than on urban ones.
No weekly re-optimisation; changes only at quarterly reviews.

items: Third-party carriers are used as overflow, not by design. On comparable routes their unit cost is 17% above in-house rounds, and service scores are two points lower.[^3] Their share is highest exactly where in-house rounds are shortest of drivers, which suggests the root cause is scheduling, not carrier capability.

items.callout: The three mechanisms compound: late loading shortens the working day, shorter days leave routes undercovered, and undercovered routes are handed to the most expensive option.
items.label: Interaction

items.h: What the data does not explain

items: Several explanations were tested and set aside. Fleet age shows no relationship with cost per parcel once route density is controlled for. Driver tenure is weakly associated with on-time delivery but not with cost. Fuel price movements affect all depots alike and do not explain the spread between them.
Two questions remain open: whether the manifest cut-off has a contractual basis, and whether the coastal depots need a separate, seasonal benchmark. Both are flagged for the pilot.

items.h: Why the order of fixes matters

items: Redrawing rounds before fixing dwell time would build new routes on an unstable loading schedule. Fixing carrier mix first would lock in volume commitments before demand per round is known.

blocks.title: Findings and recommendations
blocks.lead: Four actions, ordered by dependency rather than by size of prize.

items.title: Remove the single manifest cut-off
items.body: Stagger manifest release in three waves between 05:00 and 07:00 at the three largest depots. This cuts median dwell and lets drivers leave before peak traffic.

items.title: Redraw regional rounds to 62 stops
body: Rebuild rounds around density, not postcode boundaries, starting with the north-east cluster. Adopt weekly re-optimisation in the routing tool.
Pilot at two depots before scaling, so the savings estimate can be checked against real stop counts.

items.title: Re-tender third-party volume
items.body: Move from overflow use to two contracted carriers with committed volumes and a quality clause. Bring back in-house any route that exceeds in-house unit cost by more than 10%.

items.title: Track four measures weekly
items.body: Stops per round, median dwell, overtime share and third-party share, reported by depot to the same operating review.
